chapter_title: Deploying Smart Contracts to Local and Public Testnets

screens.title: Deploying Smart Contracts to Local and Public Testnets
screens.subtitle: From sandbox to realistic staging: deploy, verify, and stage for mainnet

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why deployment is the bridge between local development and real-world usage. Deploying means publishing your compiled contract bytecode on a blockchain so accounts and other contracts can interact with it. We start in a local development network for rapid iteration and then move to a public testnet like Sepolia to validate behavior under real network conditions, with real block times and test Ether. You'll see how Hardhat's configuration declares network endpoints and accounts, how deployment scripts use ethers. js to create and publish contracts, and why verifying your source on a block explorer matters. We'll also cover secure practices for private keys and environment variables, common mistakes such as insufficient testnet Ether or wrong constructor arguments, and the verification step that lets others audit and interact with your contract through Etherscan. By the end you will understand the end-to-end flow, the tools involved, and the safety checks that prevent costly errors. Consider one question as you proceed: which environment minimises risk for the next change you plan to deploy?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Deploy locally first for fast iteration, then deploy to a public testnet to validate in realistic conditions before considering mainnet.

screens.title: What Deploying a Contract Means
screens.subtitle: Publishing compiled bytecode so it becomes a blockchain account

narration.text: Deployment is the act of publishing your contract's compiled bytecode and metadata to a blockchain so that it gets an address and becomes callable by accounts and other contracts. Practically, you compile your Solidity source to bytecode, prepare a transaction that includes that bytecode, and sign it with the deployer's private key. The network mines or processes the transaction, and once it is confirmed, your contract receives an address. A concrete example is deploying a Counter contract: the deployment returns a contract address and you can call increment or read the counter value via that address. A common misconception is that deployment is instantaneous and free; on public networks it costs gas and requires confirmations. Another mistake is assuming the deployed bytecode can easily be changed — contracts are immutable once deployed, so thorough testing before public deployment is important. The core takeaway is that deployment converts local artifacts into a persistent, addressable on-chain service ready for real interactions and audit. How would you check that your deployed contract is the expected version before interacting with it? What Deploying a Contract Means means deployment publishes compiled bytecode as a contract account with an address; it is permanent and costs gas on public networks.. In practical terms, publishing compiled bytecode so it becomes a blockchain account. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deploy definition
keyIdea.text: Deployment publishes compiled bytecode as a contract account with an address; it is permanent and costs gas on public networks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What Deploying a Contract Means
Definition

Deployment packages compiled bytecode into a signed transaction so the blockchain can create a contract account at an address.

Concrete Example

Deploying a Counter contract returns an address. You then call functions by sending transactions to that address.

Common Misconception

Deployment is not free or reversible on public networks. Treat deployed contracts as immutable artifacts.

Why it matters

Only deployed contracts can be used by end users and other contracts; deployment is the gateway to real usage and audits.

Key Takeaway

Deployment makes a contract addressable and permanent on the chosen network; choose your network carefully.

Annotated Flow
1
Compile
Solidity source to bytecode and ABI.
2
Create transaction
Include bytecode and constructor args in the deploy transaction.
3
Sign & send
Use private key to sign; network processes the transaction and assigns an address.
4
Confirm
After confirmations, the contract is live and callable at its address.

screens.title: Local Development Networks
screens.subtitle: Fast, resettable sandboxes: Hardhat Network and Ganache

narration.text: Local development networks are private blockchain instances that run on your machine and are designed for speed and control. Hardhat Network and Ganache allow instant block mining, unlimited test Ether, and easy state resets. This makes them ideal when you are iterating on contracts and tests: transactions confirm immediately, you can snapshot and revert state, and you do not pay real gas. For example, when you run your unit tests in Hardhat, it spins up an in-memory node that processes transactions instantly. A common misconception is to assume behavior on a local network mirrors a public network in timing and congestion; it does not. Local networks are deterministic and isolated, so they won't reveal how your contracts behave under network latency or pending transactions from other users. Use local networks for rapid debugging, then move to a public testnet to observe real gas usage and confirmation times before wider staging. The essential practice is to iterate locally, then validate publicly. Local Development Networks means use local networks for rapid, cost-free iterations and deterministic testing; move to testnets for realistic validation.. In practical terms, fast, resettable sandboxes: hardhat network and ganache. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Public Testnets: Sepolia and Goerli
screens.subtitle: Realistic, public stages that mimic mainnet behavior

narration.text: Public testnets simulate the Ethereum mainnet while using test Ether that has no monetary value. Sepolia and Goerli are two such networks; Sepolia is the recommended testnet in our material. They run real consensus and have realistic block times, transaction fees, and network congestion, which helps you understand how your DApp behaves under real-world conditions. For example, when you deploy to Sepolia you'll pay gas in Sepolia testnet Ether and experience confirmation delays similar to mainnet. Testnets also let you interact with contracts deployed by others, uncovering integration issues and permission or compatibility problems. A misconception is treating testnet Ether as identical to local Ether; testnet Ether must be obtained from a faucet and can be scarce for accounts, so plan funding for your deployer. Use testnets as a staging ground: they sit between local testing and mainnet, giving you confidence without financial risk. Before you deploy, ensure your deployer account on Sepolia has sufficient testnet Ether and that your RPC URL corresponds to Sepolia's endpoint. Public Testnets: Sepolia and Goerli means use public testnets to validate contracts under realistic network conditions and interactions with other contracts.. In practical terms, realistic, public stages that mimic mainnet behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Configuring hardhat.config.js
screens.subtitle: Declare networks, compiler, and etherscan settings from environment variables

narration.text: Hardhat's main configuration file defines the compiler version, networks, and plugin settings your project uses. To deploy to multiple networks you add network entries with an RPC URL and account private keys. The recommended pattern is to load sensitive values from environment variables with a library like dotenv; that keeps them out of source control. For example, you can set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY in a. env file and reference them in hardhat. config. js. Also include your Etherscan A P I key for verification. A common error is hardcoding a private key or forgetting to add. env to. gitignore, which risks exposing credentials. Another frequent mistake is mismatched chainId: ensure your network object uses the correct chainId for Sepolia. Finally, the config should still include the hardhat target for local testing. This configuration supports a workflow where tests run on hardhat network, and deployment scripts target sepolia when you pass --network sepolia. Always validate that process. env values are defined before relying on them at runtime. Configuring hardhat.config.js means hardhat.config.js centralises compiler, network, and plugin settings; load sensitive data from .env to avoid leaks.. In practical terms, declare networks, compiler, and etherscan settings from environment variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config file role
keyIdea.text: hardhat.config.js centralises compiler, network, and plugin settings; load sensitive data from .env to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Configuring hardhat.config.js
Key fields for deployment
  • solidity: compiler version to ensure bytecode compatibility
  • networks: list of network objects with url, accounts, and chainId
  • etherscan: apiKey for contract verification
Security note

Never hardcode PRIVATE_KEY in the config. Use dotenv to load values from a local .env file kept out of version control.

Example snippet
// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL;
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.19",
  networks: {
    hardhat: {},
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL || "",
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111,
    },
  },
  etherscan: {
    apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY,
  }
};

screens.title: Managing Environment Variables and Private Keys
screens.subtitle: Use .env to load secrets and keep them out of source control

narration.text: Environment variables are the secure bridge between your local machine and the configuration file in your project. Using dotenv, you put secrets like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, PRIVATE_KEY, and ETHERSCAN_API_KEY into a. env file in the project root and then reference process. env. VARIABLE in hardhat. config. js. The crucial security rule is never to commit. env to version control; add it to. gitignore. A concrete example is creating a. env with your Alchemy or Infura endpoint as SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and the deployer private key as PRIVATE_KEY. If a developer accidentally commits a. env with a private key, the exposed key can be used by anyone to drain funds or manipulate contracts. Immediate remediation steps include moving funds from the compromised account to a new key, rotating any exposed A P I keys, and removing the file from the repository history. Another best practice is to use a separate minimal-fund deployer account for testnets and hardware wallets for mainnet deployments. This minimizes blast radius if a key is leaked. Always validate process. env values at runtime and fail fast with a helpful message when required variables are missing.

keyIdea.title: Env security
keyIdea.text: Store RPC URLs and private keys in a .env and add .env to .gitignore; rotate keys immediately if exposed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Managing Environment Variables
.env example
# .env
SEPOLIA_RPC_URL="https://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_ALCHEMY_KEY"
PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_METAMASK_PRIVATE_KEY_HERE"
ETHERSCAN_API_KEY="YOUR_ETHERSCAN_API_KEY"
If exposed
  1. Move funds to a new account immediately.
  2. Rotate API keys and remove the file from repo history.
  3. Update .gitignore and future-proof your workflow.
Best practices
  • Use a dedicated deployer account with limited funds for testnets.
  • Validate that environment variables are present at runtime and fail with clear errors.
  • For mainnet deployments prefer hardware wallets or secure key management systems.
Pro tip

Log the deployer address and balance at the start of your script to confirm the correct account is used and funded.

screens.title: Writing a Deployment Script with ethers.js
screens.subtitle: ContractFactory, deploy, await deployed — logging helpful diagnostics

narration.text: Deployment scripts are small JavaScript files that use the Hardhat runtime and ethers. js to publish a contract. A typical script gets the deployer signer, logs the deployer address and balance, obtains a ContractFactory for the contract, and calls deploy followed by awaiting deployed to confirm the transaction. This logging is important: it makes it clear which account signed the transaction and whether it had enough testnet Ether. For example, scripts/deploy. js begins by calling ethers. getSigners(), then prints the address and balance. It then calls getContractFactory('Counter'), deploys, and awaits the deployed instance, finally logging the deployed address. A misconception is that deploy returns immediately with a usable contract — you must await deployed to ensure deployment has been mined. Another possible pitfall is forgetting to pass constructor arguments if the contract requires them. Always include clear console logs and error handling in your script, and ensure you pass --network sepolia when deploying to that network. This simple structure supports reliable and debuggable deployments. Writing a Deployment Script with ethers.js means get signer, log address and balance, use contractfactory, call deploy and await deployed; include constructor args when required.. In practical terms, contractfactory, deploy, await deployed — logging helpful diagnostics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script essentials
keyIdea.text: Get signer, log address and balance, use ContractFactory, call deploy and await deployed; include constructor args when required.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Writing a Deployment Script
scripts/deploy.js
// scripts/deploy.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();

  console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address);
  console.log("Account balance:", (await deployer.getBalance()).toString());

  const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
  const counter = await Counter.deploy();

  await counter.deployed();

  console.log("Counter contract deployed to:", counter.address);
}

main()
  .then(() => process.exit(0))
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exit(1);
  });
Explanation
  • ethers.getSigners() returns accounts available to Hardhat or the configured network.
  • Logging the deployer and balance catches funding mistakes early.
  • Call deploy with constructor args if required, then await deployed() to confirm mining.
Common mistake

Forgetting constructor arguments or not awaiting deployed leads to confusing errors or interacting with an unmined contract.

screens.title: Running Deployment Commands
screens.subtitle: Local run and targeted network deployments with --network

narration.text: Running your deployment script differs slightly depending on the target network. For a local test deployment use npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js which uses the default Hardhat Network. For a public testnet such as Sepolia include --network sepolia: npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network sepolia. The difference is that Hardhat connects to a remote RPC provider using the URL and accounts defined in hardhat. config. js. Before you run the command, ensure the deployer account has sufficient testnet Ether and that your SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY are correctly set in your environment. Also confirm chainId matches the intended network. When you run the public deployment, watch the console logs for the account balance, transaction submission, and the deployed contract address. If the script fails with an authentication error, check the RPC key and private key are valid. Another runtime pitfall is mixing networks: deploying with the wrong --network value can send transactions you didn't intend, so double-check the command before pressing enter. After a successful run, copy the contract address for verification and record the transaction hash for auditability. Running Deployment Commands means use npx hardhat run locally; add --network sepolia to target sepolia and ensure deployer is funded.. In practical terms, local run and targeted network deployments with --network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Verifying Contracts on Etherscan
screens.subtitle: Make your source public and interactable using Hardhat verification

narration.text: Verification publishes your contract's source code and metadata on a block explorer so others can read, audit, and interact with it. Hardhat integrates with Etherscan through the etherscan plugin and requires an A P I key stored in your environment. After deployment, use npx hardhat verify --network sepolia followed by any constructor arguments in the exact order and format used during deployment. For example, if your contract's constructor takes an initialSupply of 1000000, you must pass that same value to the verify command. A frequent mistake is omitting constructor arguments or giving them in the wrong format, which causes verification to fail. Verification also depends on matching compiler settings and optimization flags in your config. If verification fails, review the solidity version and settings in hardhat. config. js and confirm the exact constructor signature. Once verified, the contract's explorer page shows a Contract tab with source code and an interface to call read and write functions, which aids collaboration and auditability. Verifying Contracts on Etherscan means verification publishes source for audit and enables explorer-based interaction; include constructor args exactly when verifying.. In practical terms, make your source public and interactable using hardhat verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Verification publishes source for audit and enables explorer-based interaction; include constructor args exactly when verifying.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Verifying Contracts
Verification command
# Example verify command
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0xAbCd...1234 1000000

Include constructor arguments after the address in the same order and type used during deployment. If there are no constructor arguments, omit them.

Troubleshooting
  • Confirm solidity version and optimizer settings match your build.
  • Double-check constructor argument types and order.
  • Ensure ETHERSCAN_API_KEY is set in .env and referenced in hardhat.config.js.
Result

A successful verification shows source on the explorer and an interface to interact with contract functions publicly.

screens.title: Common Deployment Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid exposure, mismatched networks, and incorrect constructor arguments

narration.text: Many deployment failures come from a handful of familiar errors. First, insufficient testnet Ether blocks deployment; always check your deployer's balance in the script before sending a transaction. Second, incorrect RPC URL or private key leads to authentication errors or sending transactions from the wrong account. Third, forgetting to add. env to. gitignore risks committing secrets. Fourth, incorrect constructor arguments will break verification or produce a different deployed state than intended. Finally, a critical safety issue is accidentally targeting mainnet when you meant Sepolia; this can cost real money and expose vulnerabilities. To mitigate these risks: log the deployer address and balance at script start, validate process. env variables and fail if any are missing, use a dedicated deployer account with minimal funds on testnets, and double-check your --network argument when running deployment commands. For production mainnet deployments prefer hardware wallets or secure key management and run multiple audits and testnet deployments first. These practices reduce the chances of irreversible or costly mistakes. Common Deployment Mistakes and Safety Notes means check funding, verify rpc and keys, keep .env out of repo, pass correct constructor args, and confirm target network.. In practical terms, avoid exposure, mismatched networks, and incorrect constructor arguments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mistakes to avoid
keyIdea.text: Check funding, verify RPC and keys, keep .env out of repo, pass correct constructor args, and confirm target network.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Common Mistakes & Safety
Common mistakes
  • Insufficient testnet Ether in the deployer account.
  • Typing mistakes in RPC URL or private key.
  • Committing .env to version control.
  • Wrong or missing constructor arguments during verification.
  • Deploying to the wrong network (mainnet vs testnet).
Safety checklist
  1. Confirm deployer address and balance in logs.
  2. Keep .env in .gitignore and rotate keys if exposed.
  3. Use a minimal-fund deployer for testnets; hardware wallets for mainnet.
  4. Double-check --network before running deployment commands.
Urgent warning

Accidentally deploying to mainnet can have irreversible financial consequences; verify every step for production deployments.

  2. Fund your deployer address with Sepolia testnet Ether from a faucet.
  3. Update hardhat.config.js to read values from process.env and add sepolia network with chainId 11155111.
  4. Write scripts/deployWallet.js, log deployer address and balance, deploy Wallet, and await deployed.
  5. Run npx hardhat run scripts/deployWallet.js --network sepolia and copy the contract address.
  6. Verify: npx hardhat verify --network sepolia [constructor args].
Hint

If Wallet has no constructor args, omit them in the verify command. If it does, pass them in exact order and type.

Why this helps

Following the checklist reduces risk and makes results reproducible for reviewers and auditors.

These points form a practical checklist for safe, repeatable deployments.
